question:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

A. It is imperative that he B. understands the severity of the situation C. and that he makes D. a clear, concise, and decisive statement to the press.
option_2: understands the severity of the situation
option_4: a clear, concise, and decisive statement to the press.
solution_text:
The correct answer is understands the severity of the situation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the structure "It is imperative that..." which expresses necessity/urgency and requires the subjunctive mood.

• In the subjunctive mood, the verb stays in its base (bare) form for every subject. So "he understands" must become "he understand".

• Part B "understands the severity of the situation" is therefore the error; it should read "understand the severity of the situation".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Subjunctive-triggering words: imperative, essential, necessary, crucial, important, vital, suggest, recommend, insist, demand, propose.

• Rule: It is imperative/essential that + subject + base verb (e.g., It is essential that she be present).

 

NOTE

• A, C and D are grammatically correct: "It is imperative that he", "and that he makes" (parallel base-form use in reported clause is fine here) and the correctly punctuated list in D contain no error, so the only fault lies in the singular present verb in Part B.

question:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

A. The new employee B. seems to be C. a fast learner D. and more smarter than the last one
option_4: and more smarter than the last one
solution_text:
The correct answer is and more smarter than the last one.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Smart" is a one-syllable adjective; its comparative degree is formed by adding "-er" → "smarter".

• Using "more" with "smarter" is a double comparative, which is grammatically incorrect.

• Part D should be "and smarter than the last one".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Degrees of comparison: use "-er/-est" for short adjectives (smart, tall, fast) and "more/most" for longer ones (beautiful, difficult).

• Never combine both: avoid "more smarter", "most easiest", "more better".

 

NOTE

• A "The new employee", B "seems to be" and C "a fast learner" are all correct; the double comparative in D is the sole error.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate preposition:

She persisted _____ all obstacles and criticism, proving her detractors wrong
option_4: despite
solution_text:
The correct answer is through.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "persist" collocates with "through" to mean continuing steadily in spite of difficulty — "persist through all obstacles".

• "Through" conveys moving/continuing from one side of the difficulties to the other, which fits "obstacles and criticism".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Collocation: persist through hardship; persist in an effort/belief; persist with a plan.

• "Detractors" = people who criticise or belittle someone.

 

NOTE

• "against" does not idiomatically follow persist here; "across" refers to going over a surface/place; "despite" is a preposition of concession but "persisted despite all obstacles" would need a different reading and is less apt than "persisted through" for continued action.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate phrasal verb:

The startup failed to _____ the expectations it had generated among investors.
option_4: live over
solution_text:
The correct answer is live up to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Live up to" means to reach or fulfil a standard, hope, or expectation.

• The startup "failed to live up to the expectations" — i.e., it could not meet what investors expected.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• live up to (expectations/reputation) = meet a standard.

• live down = make people forget something embarrassing over time.

• live through = survive/experience a difficult period.

 

NOTE

• "live down" (forget a shame), "live through" (survive an ordeal) and "live over" (not a standard idiom) do not fit the sense of meeting expectations.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word
option_4: Adverciti
solution_text:
The correct answer is Adversity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Adversity" (ad-ver-si-ty), meaning difficulties or misfortune.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Adversity (noun) = a state of hardship; synonyms: hardship, misfortune, trouble, distress.

• Related: adverse (adj.) = unfavourable.

 

NOTE

• "Advercity", "Adverisity" and "Adverciti" are all misspellings.

question:
Which of the following sentences uses the word "tear" with the same meaning as in the following sentence?

"A single tear rolled down her cheek"
option_1: He carefully tried not to tear the delicate fabric.
option_2: The little girl's tear brought her mother running
option_3: Be careful not to tear the pages of the old book.
option_4: The sharp edge of the paper can easily tear when handled roughly
solution_text:
The correct answer is The little girl's tear brought her mother running.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In "A single tear rolled down her cheek", "tear" (rhymes with "beer") is a noun meaning a drop of liquid from the eye.

• Option 2, "The little girl's tear brought her mother running", uses "tear" in exactly this sense — a drop from the eye.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• "tear" is a homograph: /tɪər/ = drop from the eye (noun); /tɛər/ = to rip apart (verb).

• Context decides the meaning and pronunciation.

 

NOTE

• Options 1, 3 and 4 all use "tear" in the sense of ripping/pulling apart (fabric, pages, paper), which is the verb meaning, not the eye-drop meaning.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word
option_4: Precarious
solution_text:
The correct answer is Precarious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Precarious" (pre-ca-ri-ous), meaning uncertain, risky, or unstable.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Precarious (adj.) = not securely held, dangerously likely to fall or fail; synonyms: risky, insecure, unstable, uncertain.

• Noun form: precariousness.

 

NOTE

• "Precurious", "Pricarious" and "Precarus" are all incorrect spellings.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions based on it:

One of the biggest ethical dilemmas of the twenty-first century is brought up by the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into modern combat, particularly in the form of autonomous weapons systems (AWS). The promise of strategic advantage is pitted against fundamental ethical principles in the fiercely debated issue of whether or not such "killer robots" should be allowed in combat. Supporters contend that autonomous weapons might decrease the loss of human life, since they do not fear, become tired, or suffer the emotional stress that can cause human mistakes in combat. They also might be able to operate with more accuracy and rapidity in an unpredictable environment, which could decrease civilian casualties.

The ethical arguments are serious, nonetheless. The most compelling argument is the transfer of the life-and-death decision-making from a human to a machine. Opponents contend that a computer, however sophisticated, could never have the moral calculus, compassion, or comprehension of human dignity to make such judgments. This creates an important question of accountability: in the event that an autonomous weapon kills without authorisation, who has the moral and legal culpability? Is it the programmer who wrote the algorithm, the commander who sent the system out, or the state that legitimised its use? The secrecy of AI's decision-making process, commonly known as a "black box," also adds to the difficulty in assigning blame. This built-in absence of clear moral and legal norms tests the very foundations of the international laws of armed conflict. Essentially, the debate about autonomous weapons puts us in a position of considering not only the technology but also human responsibility, judgment, and the ethical limits we are prepared to place on the waging of war.

 

Which of the following is the most compelling ethical argument against autonomous weapons in combat?
option_1: The potential for increased civilian casualties
option_2: The speed at which autonomous weapons operate
option_3: The transfer of life-and-death decision-making to machines
option_4: The lack of accountability in AI decisions
solution_text:
The correct answer is The transfer of life-and-death decision-making to machines.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states directly: "The most compelling argument is the transfer of the life-and-death decision-making from a human to a machine."

• Hence the most compelling ethical argument against autonomous weapons is the transfer of such decisions to machines.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• RC tip: for "most compelling / main argument" questions, locate the exact superlative phrase in the text ("most compelling argument").

 

NOTE

• Options 1 and 4 are concerns mentioned in the passage but are not named as the "most compelling" one; option 2 (speed) is actually cited as an advantage claimed by supporters, not an argument against.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

• The passage says the secrecy of AI's decision-making, "commonly known as a 'black box,' also adds to the difficulty in assigning blame."

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

• "culpability" = responsibility for a fault or wrong; blameworthiness.

 

NOTE

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are not the concern linked to the "black box"; speed and reduced casualties are framed elsewhere as advantages, and hindering efficiency is not the point made about the black box.

option_3: They ensure that no human is ever at risk in combat

solution_text:
The correct answer is They act with more accuracy and rapidity.

• Supporters argue autonomous weapons "might be able to operate with more accuracy and rapidity in an unpredictable environment."

• This is the pro-autonomous-weapons argument stated in the passage, so option 4 is correct per the official key.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• RC tip: match the option to the exact wording supporters use ("more accuracy and rapidity").

 

NOTE

• Reducing civilian casualties (1) is only a possible consequence of that accuracy, not the argument itself; "more humane warfare" (2) and "no human ever at risk" (3) are overstatements not made in the text.

question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: Below the belt
option_4: Unfair or unjust behavior
solution_text:
The correct answer is Unfair or unjust behavior.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "below the belt" means an unfair, unjust, or cruel act or remark.

• It comes from boxing, where hitting an opponent below the belt line is against the rules.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Example: "Mocking his stammer was really below the belt."

• Synonymous expressions: unfair, unsporting, a low blow.

 

NOTE

• Options 1, 2 and 3 take the phrase literally (a light hit, care, a boxing punch) and miss its figurative "unfair" meaning.

question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: Star-crossed lovers
option_4: Happy lovers
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lovers whose relationship is doomed.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Star-crossed lovers" refers to a couple whose relationship is doomed to fail, as if the stars (fate) are against them.

• The phrase was popularised by Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• "star-crossed" = thwarted by ill fortune; ill-fated.

• Rooted in the old belief that the position of stars decides destiny.

 

NOTE

• "Facing many challenges" (2) is weaker than "doomed"; "very successful" (3) and "happy" (4) are opposite in sense.

question: Select the most appropriate antonym of the word: Sporadic
option_4: Intermittent
solution_text:
The correct answer is Frequent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Sporadic" means occurring at irregular intervals; scattered or occasional.

• Its antonym is "Frequent", meaning happening often and regularly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Sporadic synonyms: occasional, intermittent, infrequent, irregular.

• Antonyms: frequent, constant, continual, regular.

 

NOTE

• "Infrequent", "Occasional" and "Intermittent" are synonyms of sporadic, not antonyms.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for:

A place where dead bodies are kept for examination
option_4: Clinic
solution_text:
The correct answer is Morgue.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Morgue" (also mortuary) is a place where dead bodies are kept for identification, examination, or until burial.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Morgue / mortuary = building where corpses are kept.

• Autopsy/post-mortem = examination of a dead body.

 

NOTE

• A "Cemetery" is where the dead are buried; a "Hospital" and "Clinic" treat living patients — none is for keeping bodies for examination.

question: Select the most appropriate antonym of the word: Fastidious
option_4: Perceptive
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sloppy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Fastidious" means very attentive to detail, hard to please, and excessively particular about neatness.

• Its antonym is "Sloppy", meaning careless, untidy, or lacking attention to detail.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Fastidious synonyms: meticulous, fussy, particular, scrupulous.

• Antonyms: sloppy, careless, slovenly, disorganised.

 

NOTE

• "Meticulous" and "Fussy" are synonyms of fastidious; "Perceptive" (insightful) is unrelated.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for:

A person who performs magic tricks
option_4: Illusionist
solution_text:
The correct answer is Magician.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Magician" is a person who performs magic tricks, especially as entertainment.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Magician = entertainer performing tricks/illusions.

• Compare: conjurer (one who does conjuring tricks).

 

NOTE

• A "Sorcerer" and "Wizard" are associated with supernatural/occult powers, not stage tricks; an "Illusionist" specialises in large-scale illusions but "Magician" is the standard one-word answer for one who performs magic tricks.

question:
Change the following sentence into the Active form.

The city council's decision is thought to be influenced by powerful lobbying groups.
option_1: Powerful lobbying groups think that the city council's decision is influenced
option_2: Powerful lobbying groups are thought to influence the city council's decision.
option_3: People think that powerful lobbying groups influence the city council's decision.
option_4: The city council thinks that powerful lobbying groups influence the decision
solution_text:
The correct answer is People think that powerful lobbying groups influence the city council's decision..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passive "is thought to be influenced by" has an implied general subject ("people/it is thought").

• Converting to active, the doer of "thinking" becomes "People", and "powerful lobbying groups" become the active subject of "influence": "People think that powerful lobbying groups influence the city council's decision."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Structure: "It is thought that X" / "X is thought to..." → Active: "People think that X..."

• Keep the tense (present) and the true doer (lobbying groups) as the subject of the inner clause.

 

NOTE

• Option 1 wrongly leaves "is influenced" passive; option 2 stays passive ("are thought to"); option 4 changes the meaning by making the city council the thinker.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect voice.

The guide said, "We will be exploring the ruins all morning."
option_1: The guide said that they would be exploring the ruins all morning.
option_2: The guide said that they will be exploring the ruins all morning
option_3: The guide said that we would be exploring the ruins all morning.
option_4: The guide said that they were exploring the ruins all morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is The guide said that they would be exploring the ruins all morning..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In indirect speech, "will" changes to "would" and the pronoun "We" changes to "they" (the guide's group).

• The future continuous "will be exploring" becomes "would be exploring": "The guide said that they would be exploring the ruins all morning."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Backshift rules: will → would; can → could; is/are → was/were.

• Pronoun change: We → they (when the speaker is being reported by another).

 

NOTE

• Option 2 keeps "will" (no backshift); option 3 keeps "we" (wrong pronoun); option 4 changes "would be exploring" to "were exploring", altering the tense/aspect.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

Except for you and me, no one knew Radha.
option_1: Except for you and I, no one knew Radha
option_2: Except for you and me, no one knew Radha
option_3: Except you and I, no one knew Radha
option_4: Except for I and you, no one knew Radha
solution_text:
The correct answer is Except for you and I, no one knew Radha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As per the official answer key, the highlighted part is best replaced by "Except for you and I, no one knew Radha", which supplies the missing subject "no one" and completes the sentence.

• (Grammar note: after the preposition "for" the objective form "you and me" is normally expected, so Option 2 is arguably the more textbook-correct choice; however, the highlighted official key marks Option 1.)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• SSC tip: the sentence needs a main subject ("no one") plus the verb "knew"; all valid options add "no one knew Radha".

• After a preposition, pronouns generally take the objective case (me, him, us), e.g., "between you and me".

 

NOTE

• Option 3 drops "for" (Except you and I); option 4 uses an unnatural order "I and you" and wrong case; Option 2, though grammatically sound, is not the marked key.

question:
Choose the correct passive voice transformation of the sentence:

Why did the brilliant detective suddenly solve the complex mystery?
option_1: Why was the complex mystery suddenly solved by the brilliant detective?
option_2: Why was the complex mystery suddenly been solved by the brilliant detective?
option_3: Why has the complex mystery been suddenly solved by the brilliant detective?
option_4: Why did the complex mystery be solved by the brilliant detective?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Why was the complex mystery suddenly solved by the brilliant detective?.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The active sentence is simple past interrogative: "Why did the detective solve...?"

• Passive of simple past = was/were + past participle. The object "the complex mystery" becomes the subject: "Why was the complex mystery suddenly solved by the brilliant detective?"

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Simple past passive: was/were + V3.

• In Wh- questions, keep the question word first, then the passive auxiliary.

 

NOTE

• Option 2 wrongly adds "been" after "was"; option 3 uses present perfect "has been" (wrong tense); option 4 keeps "did...be", which is ungrammatical.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct voice.

The traveler explained that he was going to visit several historic sites on his trip.
option_1: The traveler said, "He was going to visit several historic sites on his trip."
option_2: The traveler said, "He is going to visit several historic sites on his trip."
option_3: The traveler explained, "I was going to visit several historic sites on my trip."
option_4: The traveler said, "I am going to visit several historic sites on my trip."
solution_text:
The correct answer is The traveler said, "I am going to visit several historic sites on my trip.".

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Converting indirect to direct speech, we reverse the backshift: "was going" returns to "am going", and "he/his" returns to the first person "I/my".

• The correct direct form is: The traveler said, "I am going to visit several historic sites on my trip."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Indirect → Direct: reverse tense backshift (was → am/is) and restore original pronouns (he → I, his → my).

• Use quotation marks and a capital letter to begin the reported words.

 

NOTE

• Options 1 and 2 keep the third-person "He" (not restored to "I"); option 3 keeps the past "was going" instead of "am going".

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a meaningful and grammatically correct paragraph:

P. He disassembled the old engine with care, marking each component precisely.

Q. He torqued the bolts to the precise specifications, put in new gaskets, and replaced old parts.

R. After reassembling the engine, he put it back in the vehicle and reattached all of the hoses.

S. On the first turn of the key, the engine flickered to life and resumed its flawless operation.
option_4: Q, P, R, S
solution_text:
The correct answer is P, Q, R, S.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The logical sequence of repairing an engine: first take it apart (P), then fix/replace parts (Q), then reassemble and refit it (R), and finally start it successfully (S).

• P → Q → R → S gives a coherent chronological paragraph.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Para-jumble tip: follow the natural time order of actions (disassemble → repair → reassemble → test).

• The closing sentence (S) describes the final result, so it must come last.

 

NOTE

• Sequences starting with R, S or Q break the chronology (you cannot reassemble or start the engine before disassembling and repairing it).

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a meaningful and grammatically correct paragraph:

P: As a result, the software significantly improved operational efficiency across departments

Q: The team worked tirelessly, refining the code and testing each feature for compatibility.

R: It was designed to simplify daily tasks and provide real-time data analysis.

S: A groundbreaking new software was developed to streamline workflow and increase productivity.
option_4: S, P, Q, R
solution_text:
The correct answer is S, R, Q, P.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• S introduces the topic (a new software was developed), R elaborates its purpose ("It was designed to..."), Q describes the team's work on it, and P gives the concluding result ("As a result...").

• The coherent order is S → R → Q → P.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information (Exam-oriented)

• Para-jumble tip: the opening sentence introduces the subject (S); "It was designed" (R) must follow the noun it refers to; "As a result" (P) signals the concluding effect, so it comes last.

 

NOTE

• Options beginning with P or R are wrong because "As a result" cannot open the paragraph and "It" in R needs an antecedent (the software in S) before it.
